sources.title: Human History Map 1715 CE borders

sources.title: De la Fuente and colleagues, genomes of late maritime hunter-gatherers
sources.note: Ancient and modern genomes distinguish Chono, Kawesqar and Yaghan histories and evidence limits.

sources.title: Nakatsuka and colleagues, ancient genomes in South Patagonia
sources.note: Genome-wide data separate maritime and terrestrial populations, geography and technological change.

sources.title: Colonese and colleagues, dietary resilience in Tierra del Fuego
sources.note: Human and faunal isotopes trace diverse marine diets across pre-contact and historical contexts.

sources.title: Schiavini, sea lions as an energetic resource in Tierra del Fuego
sources.note: Beagle Channel fauna show pinnipeds supplied crucial fat and energy before commercial depletion.

sources.title: Pal, Alvarez and Briz Godino, Lanashuaia II animal materials
sources.note: Technological study identifies bird, guanaco and marine-mammal bone tools and ornaments.

sources.title: Vila and colleagues, social use of space in a shell midden
sources.note: Túnel VII spatial analysis tests ring midden, central hut and historical household interpretations.

sources.title: Eidshaug and colleagues, remote sensing Beagle Channel middens
sources.note: Survey and remote sensing distinguish ring dwellings, domes, sheltered harbors and later canoe runways.

sources.title: Zangrando, subsistence and landscape use in the Beagle Channel
sources.note: Five shell middens reveal changing proportions of marine mammals, fish, birds and land prey.

sources.title: Mansur and Lasa, functional diversity at Túnel I
sources.note: Use-wear, context and faunal counts test specialized tasks within one archaeological component.

sources.title: Zangrando and colleagues, shell collection zones in the Beagle Channel
sources.note: Mollusk measurements at Túnel VII and Lanashuaia reconstruct localized gathering choices.

sources.title: Fiore and colleagues, Yendegaia rockshelter and social interaction
sources.note: Dated occupation, first island rock art and motif comparison reveal interaction without uniform belief.

sources.title: Morello and colleagues, barriers and settlement in Tierra del Fuego
sources.note: Archaeology separates earlier terrestrial settlement from later maritime technologies and coexistence.

sources.title: Borrero, archaeology of canoe groups in the Chonos Archipelago
sources.note: Regional review emphasizes sparse surveys, obsidian transport and uncertainty in northern channels.

sources.title: Reyes and colleagues, canoe and colonial occupations at Taitao and Gulf of Penas
sources.note: Coastal surveys distinguish canoe occupations, colonial movement and uneven Chono cultural disruption.

sources.title: Reyes and Mendez, Traiguen archaeology in the northern channels
sources.note: Dated sites and human remains frame debates over Chono mobility, ancestry and regional variation.

sources.title: Borrero and colleagues, opportunistic animal resources in Patagonia
sources.note: Archaeology and historical records show flexible use of stranded whales, fish and other windfalls.

sources.title: Bas and colleagues, past and modern southern marine food webs
sources.note: Shell and predator isotopes test ecological change and the consequences of industrial exploitation.

sources.title: Alfonso-Durruty and colleagues, Cabo Nose burial
sources.note: A late Holocene burial in shell midden context combines diet isotopes and paleopathology.

sources.title: Guichon and Suby, Caleta Falsa bioarchaeology
sources.note: Six individuals include adults, a juvenile and child with localized health indicators.

sources.title: Garcia Guraieb, paleopathology in southern Patagonia
sources.note: Regional review evaluates skeletal stress, disease, preservation and contact-era change.

sources.title: Camacho and colleagues, South American paleoparasitology review
sources.note: Review reports parasite evidence at Caleta Falsa while explaining sample and diagnosis limits.

sources.title: Dominguez and colleagues, ethnobotany of Kalau Island
sources.note: Localized Kawesqar plant knowledge covers food, structures, fuel, containers and wound care.

sources.title: Franch Bach, plant management in Tierra del Fuego
sources.note: Archaeobotanical review separates direct charcoal evidence from historical Yaghan and Selknam comparison.

sources.title: UNESCO, Cape Horn Biosphere Reserve
sources.note: Institutional environmental profile covers channels, kelp, forests, tundra, glaciers and watercourses.

sources.title: Rozzi and colleagues, Cape Horn biocomplexity
sources.note: Ecology and cultural history describe rainfall gradients, marine foods and Yaghan landscape relationships.

sources.title: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino, Yaghan economy
sources.note: Museum synthesis localizes historical canoe crews, diving, paddling, fire, fishing and family mobility.

sources.title: Biblioteca Nacional de Chile, Kawesqar history and lifeways
sources.note: National-library synthesis covers hallef canoes, camps, foods, gatherings and named people.

sources.title: Servicio del Patrimonio Cultural, western Patagonia watercraft
sources.note: Museum research traces bark, sewn-plank and dugout canoe change without assuming timeless form.

sources.title: Museo Martin Gusinde Yaghan ethnographic collection
sources.note: Community-linked collection documents basket varieties, fiber technology and intergenerational knowledge.

sources.title: Servicio del Patrimonio Cultural, Yaghan basketry
sources.note: Museum study highlights individual, family and historical variation in living basket traditions.

sources.title: Fiore and colleagues, art of the Yaghan chiejaus
sources.note: Painted wood objects and historical records document a named initiation and teaching ceremony.

sources.title: Garcia Alonso, the body in Kawesqar cultural memory
sources.note: Critical historical-ethnographic synthesis covers childhood, play, hygiene, health, initiation and colonial change.

sources.title: Harambour and Barrena, plagues and futures for Yagan canoe people
sources.note: Community-centered history documents food, family groups, exchange, violence, epidemics and living futures.

sources.title: Argentina INAI, legal recognition of Yagan Paiakola
sources.note: Official recognition confirms a living Yagan community in Ushuaia and legal continuity.

sources.title: Servicio del Patrimonio Cultural, Kawesqar language council
sources.note: Community language work rejects extinction claims and documents modern vocabulary development.

sources.title: Servicio del Patrimonio Cultural, Yaghan object restitution
sources.note: Community-requested return of baskets, masks, tools and canoe model supports local teaching.

sources.title: Servicio del Patrimonio Cultural, Yagan Usi museum
sources.note: Museum account centers continuing Yaghan presence and returned archaeological and ethnographic collections.

sources.title: Argentina national monument decree on Ushuaia mission
sources.note: Official history dates Thomas Bridges, the Anglican mission and his extensive Yaghan dictionary.

sources.title: Driver, science and empire in Darwin era Tierra del Fuego
sources.note: Source-critical study reconstructs Yaghan encounters, kin groups, bark canoes and colonial collecting.

sources.title: Parmigiani and colleagues, torches in Fuegian-Patagonian societies
sources.note: Archaeology and historical comparison examine portable fire, tinder kits and task lighting.

sources.title: Riede and colleagues, hunter-gatherer children play and tool use
sources.note: Cross-cultural review supports cautious comparison for learning, toys and scaled tools.

sources.title: Hamley and colleagues, possible prehistoric activity in the Falklands
sources.note: Multi-proxy evidence raises but does not settle a hypothesis of pre-European seafaring visits.

sources.title: Halcrow and colleagues, bone density and cold adaptation hypotheses
sources.note: Bone and genomic study tests cold adaptation while grouping evidence that needs cultural caution.

sources.title: CADIC-CONICET, science at the end of the world
sources.note: Institutional research overview dates Beagle Channel occupations and changing maritime strategies.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Changing maritime atlas umbrella across western Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, circa 1500 BCE to 1880 CE.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id and display label are preserved as atlas metadata, not an ancient or modern self-name.
Thirty-five exact features form nine geometry signatures plus controls before, during the 1492 gap and after 1880.
The early four-part footprint includes sampled inland Bariloche and excludes sampled Puerto Williams and Cape Horn, so the label cannot define real cultural geography.
Chono, Kawesqar, Yaghan, Selk nam, Haush, Aonikenk and neighboring histories remain distinct and locally attributed.
Archaeological finds, scientific inference, late historical documents and living community knowledge are explicitly separated.
No written sample is supplied because no single text can represent the exact umbrella across its footprint and interval.
The 1880 endpoint records state replacement and colonization, not a shared cultural fall or extinction.
